notes.front: What is general awareness/familiarization training?
notes.back: Training that gives each hazmat employee familiarity with the HMR and the ability to recognise and identify hazmat under the hazard communication standards.
notes.explanation: It is the first of the components 172.704(a) lists, and every hazmat employee must receive it.
notes.example: Like an induction course that teaches every new starter what the warning signs on site mean, whatever their own job.
notes.evidence: Each hazmat employee shall be provided general awareness/familiarization training designed to provide familiarity with the requirements of this subchapter, and to enable the employee to recognize and identify hazardous materials consistent with the hazard communication standards of this subchapter.

notes.front: What is function-specific training?
notes.back: Training on the HMR requirements, exemptions or special permits that apply specifically to the functions the hazmat employee performs.
notes.explanation: Its content depends on the job, so a driver and a packer receive different function-specific training.
notes.example: Like job-specific instruction on a machine you will operate, but for the HMR duties of your own role.
notes.evidence: Each hazmat employee must be provided function-specific training concerning requirements of this subchapter, or exemptions or special permits issued under subchapter A of this chapter, that are specifically applicable to the functions the employee performs.

notes.front: What is safety training under 172.704(a)(3)?
notes.back: Training on emergency response information, measures to protect the employee from hazmat hazards, and methods for avoiding accidents.
notes.explanation: Each hazmat employee must receive it, and the protective measures include those the employer has put in place.
notes.example: Like a fire-safety briefing, but covering what to do with the hazmat you work with and how to avoid accidents with it.
notes.evidence: Each hazmat employee shall receive safety training concerning— (i) Emergency response information required by subpart G of part 172; (ii) Measures to protect the employee from the hazards associated with hazardous materials to which they may be exposed in the work place

notes.front: What is security awareness training?
notes.back: Training that gives each hazmat employee an awareness of the security risks of hazmat transport and of methods to enhance transportation security.
notes.explanation: It must also include a component on recognising and responding to possible security threats.
notes.example: Like a briefing on spotting suspicious behaviour at an airport, but for hazmat shipments and the people around them.
notes.evidence: Each hazmat employee must receive training that provides an awareness of security risks associated with hazardous materials transportation and methods designed to enhance transportation security. This training must also include a component covering how to recognize and respond to possible security threats.

notes.front: What is in-depth security training?
notes.back: Training on the security plan and its implementation, for hazmat employees of a person required to have a security plan under subpart I.
notes.explanation: Only employees linked to the plan need it: those who handle covered hazmat, perform related regulated functions, or implement the plan.
notes.example: Like the detailed site security procedures a guard at a secure facility learns, beyond the general awareness everyone gets.
notes.evidence: Each hazmat employee of a person required to have a security plan in accordance with subpart I of this part who handles hazardous materials covered by the plan, performs a regulated function related to the hazardous materials covered by the plan, or is responsible for implementing the plan must be trained concerning the security plan and its implementation.

notes.front: Under 172.700(b), training is a systematic program that ensures a hazmat employee has {{c1::familiarity with the general provisions}} of the HMR, among other things.
notes.explanation: This element matches general awareness/familiarization training in 172.704(a)(1).
notes.evidence: Training as used in this subpart means a systematic program that ensures a hazmat employee has familiarity with the general provisions of this subchapter

notes.front: Under 172.700(b), training must ensure a hazmat employee {{c1::is able to recognize and identify}} hazardous materials.
notes.explanation: Recognising and identifying hazmat is also part of general awareness/familiarization training.
notes.evidence: is able to recognize and identify hazardous materials, has knowledge of specific requirements of this subchapter applicable to functions performed by the employee

notes.front: Under 172.700(b), training must give a hazmat employee knowledge of the specific HMR requirements applicable to {{c1::functions performed by the employee}}.
notes.explanation: This element is delivered through function-specific training.
notes.evidence: has knowledge of specific requirements of this subchapter applicable to functions performed by the employee

notes.front: Under 172.700(b), training must give knowledge of emergency response information, {{c1::self-protection measures}} and accident prevention methods and procedures.
notes.explanation: These three subjects correspond to the three parts of safety training in 172.704(a)(3).
notes.evidence: has knowledge of emergency response information, self-protection measures and accident prevention methods and procedures (see § 172.704).

notes.front: An employer hands a new starter a copy of the HMR and says, “Read this.” Does that meet the 172.700(b) meaning of training?
notes.back: No. Training means a systematic program that ensures the employee gains the listed familiarity, recognition skills and knowledge.
notes.explanation: The definition requires a program that ensures results, and 172.702(d) separately requires testing on the subjects.
notes.evidence: Training as used in this subpart means a systematic program that ensures a hazmat employee has familiarity with the general provisions of this subchapter

notes.front: A company’s hazmat employees drive road tankers. Besides subpart H of part 172, which part holds additional training requirements for them?
notes.back: Part 177, carriage by public highway.
notes.explanation: 172.700(c) points to parts 174, 175, 176 and 177 for the additional modal training requirements, and part 177 is the highway part.
notes.evidence: Additional training requirements for the individual modes of transportation are prescribed in parts 174, 175, 176, and 177 of this subchapter.

notes.front: Under 172.701, when may a State impose stricter training requirements on motor vehicle drivers?
notes.back: Only if they do not conflict with subpart H and part 177, and apply only to drivers domiciled in that State.
notes.explanation: The section opens by calling subpart H and the modal parts minimum training requirements.
notes.evidence: For motor vehicle drivers, however, a State may impose more stringent training requirements only if those requirements— (a) Do not conflict with the training requirements in this subpart and in part 177 of this subchapter; and (b) Apply only to drivers domiciled in that State.

notes.front: A haulage firm’s new driver says he did a hazmat course years ago and will sort out his own refresher. Who must ensure he is trained under subpart H?
notes.back: A: The haulage firm, as his hazmat employer.
notes.explanation: 172.702(a) places the duty to ensure training on the hazmat employer.
notes.choices:
A) The haulage firm, as his hazmat employer
B) The driver himself
C) The Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration
D) The course provider he used before
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: the regulation puts the duty on the employer, not the employee. C is wrong: the agency issues the rules but does not train employees. D is wrong: a provider may deliver training, but the duty to ensure it stays with the employer.
notes.evidence: (a) A hazmat employer shall ensure that each of its hazmat employees is trained in accordance with the requirements prescribed in this subpart.

notes.front: Under 172.702(b), may a hazmat employee perform a regulated function before being instructed in its requirements?
notes.back: No, except under the 172.704(c)(1) initial-training provision.
notes.explanation: The exception lets a new or reassigned employee work under direct supervision while training is completed.
notes.evidence: Except as provided in § 172.704(c)(1), a hazmat employee who performs any function subject to the requirements of this subchapter may not perform that function unless instructed in the requirements of this subchapter that apply to that function.

notes.front: A packer moves to the shipping office and is told to start certifying shipping papers alone tomorrow, with no instruction and no supervisor. What does 172.702(b) say?
notes.back: C: He may not perform the function until instructed in its requirements, unless working under the 172.704(c)(1) supervision provision.
notes.explanation: 172.702(b) bars performing a regulated function before instruction, with the exception in 172.704(c)(1).
notes.choices:
A) He may start, because his packing training covers all functions
B) He may start and be trained within three years
C) He may not perform the function until instructed in its requirements, unless working under the 172.704(c)(1) supervision provision
D) He may start, as long as he is tested afterwards
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: instruction must cover the requirements that apply to the new function. B is wrong: three years is the recurrent cycle, not a grace period. D is wrong: testing does not replace instruction before the work.
notes.evidence: Except as provided in § 172.704(c)(1), a hazmat employee who performs any function subject to the requirements of this subchapter may not perform that function unless instructed in the requirements of this subchapter that apply to that function.

notes.front: A small shipper cannot run its own course. May it use a public or private training provider to meet subpart H?
notes.back: Yes. Training may be provided by the hazmat employer or by other public or private sources.
notes.explanation: 172.702(c) leaves the source of training open, but 172.702(a) keeps the duty to ensure that each hazmat employee is trained on the employer.
notes.evidence: (c) Training may be provided by the hazmat employer or other public or private sources.

notes.front: Under 172.702(d), what must a hazmat employer ensure besides training?
notes.back: That each hazmat employee is tested by appropriate means on the training subjects in 172.704.
notes.explanation: The regulation says only “appropriate means”; it sets no pass mark or test format.
notes.evidence: (d) A hazmat employer shall ensure that each of its hazmat employees is tested by appropriate means on the training subjects covered in § 172.704.

notes.front: After a training day, an employer hands out attendance certificates but gives no test of any kind. What is missing under 172.702(d)?
notes.back: A: Testing each hazmat employee by appropriate means on the 172.704 training subjects.
notes.explanation: 172.702(d) makes testing a separate duty, and the record must certify that the employee was trained and tested.
notes.choices:
A) Testing each hazmat employee by appropriate means on the 172.704 training subjects
B) A test set by the federal agency with a fixed pass mark
C) A signed statement from each employee
D) Nothing: attendance is enough
notes.choicesExplained: D is wrong: 172.702(d) requires testing as well as training. B is wrong: the regulation says “appropriate means” and sets no pass mark. C is wrong: a statement from the employee is not a test.
notes.evidence: (d) A hazmat employer shall ensure that each of its hazmat employees is tested by appropriate means on the training subjects covered in § 172.704.

notes.front: A module teaches every hazmat employee, whatever their role, how the HMR are organised and how to recognise hazmat from its markings and labels. Which component is it?
notes.back: C: General awareness/familiarization training.
notes.explanation: This component gives familiarity with the HMR and the ability to recognise and identify hazmat under the hazard communication standards.
notes.choices:
A) Security awareness training
B) Function-specific training
C) General awareness/familiarization training
D) In-depth security training
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: function-specific training is tied to the duties of one job. A is wrong: security awareness covers security risks and threats. D is wrong: in-depth security training concerns an employer’s security plan.
notes.evidence: designed to provide familiarity with the requirements of this subchapter, and to enable the employee to recognize and identify hazardous materials consistent with the hazard communication standards of this subchapter.

notes.front: Does function-specific training cover special permits?
notes.back: Yes. It covers HMR requirements, exemptions or special permits specifically applicable to the functions the employee performs.
notes.explanation: An employee working under a special permit needs training on its terms as they apply to the job.
notes.evidence: function-specific training concerning requirements of this subchapter, or exemptions or special permits issued under subchapter A of this chapter, that are specifically applicable to the functions the employee performs.

notes.front: A warehouse worker who fills drums is taught the HMR rules on selecting packagings and securing closures. Which training component is that?
notes.back: A: Function-specific training.
notes.explanation: Training on requirements specifically applicable to the functions the employee performs is function-specific training.
notes.choices:
A) Function-specific training
B) Safety training
C) General awareness/familiarization training
D) Security awareness training
notes.choicesExplained: C is wrong: general awareness is the same broad familiarity for every employee. B is wrong: safety training covers emergency response information, self-protection and accident avoidance. D is wrong: security awareness covers security risks.
notes.evidence: that are specifically applicable to the functions the employee performs.

notes.front: What may replace function-specific training on the HMR, to the extent it covers functions authorised by subpart C of part 171?
notes.back: Training on the International Civil Aviation Organization Technical Instructions and the International Maritime Dangerous Goods Code.
notes.explanation: Subpart C of part 171 authorises use of these international standards, so training on them can cover those functions.
notes.evidence: As an alternative to function-specific training on the requirements of this subchapter, training relating to the requirements of the ICAO Technical Instructions and the IMDG Code may be provided to the extent such training addresses functions authorized by subpart C of part 171

notes.front: The first subject of safety training is emergency response information required by {{c1::subpart G}} of part 172.
notes.explanation: Safety training ties to the emergency response information rules elsewhere in part 172.
notes.evidence: (i) Emergency response information required by subpart G of part 172;

notes.front: Which safety training subject includes the specific measures the hazmat employer has implemented?
notes.back: Measures to protect the employee from the hazards of hazmat they may be exposed to in the work place.
notes.explanation: This subject is partly employer-specific, because it covers the protective measures that employer has put in place.
notes.evidence: (ii) Measures to protect the employee from the hazards associated with hazardous materials to which they may be exposed in the work place, including specific measures the hazmat employer has implemented to protect employees from exposure;

notes.front: Which safety training subject gives proper package-handling procedures as its example?
notes.back: Methods and procedures for avoiding accidents.
notes.explanation: The regulation uses package handling to illustrate accident avoidance, with “such as”, so other methods count too.
notes.evidence: (iii) Methods and procedures for avoiding accidents, such as the proper procedures for handling packages containing hazardous materials.

notes.front: A session teaches loaders which gloves and respirators the company provides for the corrosive liquids they handle. Which component does it belong to?
notes.back: C: Safety training.
notes.explanation: Measures to protect employees from exposure, including those the employer has implemented, are part of safety training.
notes.choices:
A) General awareness/familiarization training
B) Security awareness training
C) Safety training
D) In-depth security training
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: general awareness covers familiarity with the HMR and recognising hazmat. B is wrong: security awareness concerns security risks and threats. D is wrong: in-depth security training concerns the security plan.
notes.evidence: Measures to protect the employee from the hazards associated with hazardous materials to which they may be exposed in the work place, including specific measures the hazmat employer has implemented to protect employees from exposure

notes.front: New hazmat employees must receive security awareness training within {{c1::90 days}} after employment.
notes.explanation: The deadline for this component is stated separately in 172.704(a)(4), and runs from the start of employment.
notes.evidence: New hazmat employees must receive the security awareness training required by this paragraph within 90 days after employment.

notes.front: A hazmat employee starts work on 1 March. By when must she have received security awareness training?
notes.back: D: Within 90 days after employment began.
notes.explanation: 172.704(a)(4) sets a 90-day limit for new hazmat employees.
notes.choices:
A) Before her first day
B) Within 30 days
C) Within three years
D) Within 90 days after employment began
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: the regulation allows up to 90 days. B is wrong: 30 days is not the stated period. C is wrong: three years is the recurrent training cycle.
notes.evidence: New hazmat employees must receive the security awareness training required by this paragraph within 90 days after employment.

notes.front: In-depth security training must include company security {{c1::objectives}}.
notes.explanation: This is the first of the five contents listed in 172.704(a)(5).
notes.evidence: Security training must include company security objectives, organizational security struc- ture, specific security procedures, specific security duties and responsibilities for each employee, and specific actions to be taken by each employee in the event of a security breach.

notes.front: In-depth security training must include the organisational security {{c1::structure}}.
notes.explanation: Employees learn how security is organised in the company, not only what to do.
notes.evidence: Security training must include company security objectives, organizational security struc- ture, specific security procedures, specific security duties and responsibilities for each employee, and specific actions to be taken by each employee in the event of a security breach.

notes.front: In-depth security training must include specific security {{c1::procedures}}.
notes.explanation: The word “specific” ties the training to the company’s own plan.
notes.evidence: Security training must include company security objectives, organizational security struc- ture, specific security procedures, specific security duties and responsibilities for each employee, and specific actions to be taken by each employee in the event of a security breach.

notes.front: In-depth security training must include specific security duties and responsibilities {{c1::for each employee}}.
notes.explanation: The duties are set per employee, not only for the company as a whole.
notes.evidence: Security training must include company security objectives, organizational security struc- ture, specific security procedures, specific security duties and responsibilities for each employee, and specific actions to be taken by each employee in the event of a security breach.

notes.front: In-depth security training must include specific actions to be taken by each employee in the event of a {{c1::security breach}}.
notes.explanation: This is the last of the five contents, covering what each employee does when security fails.
notes.evidence: Security training must include company security objectives, organizational security struc- ture, specific security procedures, specific security duties and responsibilities for each employee, and specific actions to be taken by each employee in the event of a security breach.

notes.front: An in-depth security course covers company security objectives, security structure, procedures and each employee’s duties, but not what to do if security is breached. What is missing?
notes.back: The specific actions each employee must take in the event of a security breach.
notes.explanation: 172.704(a)(5) lists breach actions as the last of the five required contents of in-depth security training.
notes.evidence: specific security duties and responsibilities for each employee, and specific actions to be taken by each employee in the event of a security breach.

notes.front: A company must have a security plan under subpart I. Which of its staff needs in-depth security training?
notes.back: B: A dispatcher who performs a regulated function related to the hazmat the plan covers.
notes.explanation: In-depth training is for employees who handle covered hazmat, perform a related regulated function, or are responsible for implementing the plan.
notes.choices:
A) A canteen worker with no hazmat duties
B) A dispatcher who performs a regulated function related to the hazmat the plan covers
C) Every employee of any shipper, plan or no plan
D) Only the manager who wrote the plan
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: the rule reaches only hazmat employees linked to the plan. C is wrong: it applies only to employees of a person required to have a security plan. D is wrong: handlers and those performing related regulated functions are covered too.
notes.evidence: who handles hazardous materials covered by the plan, performs a regulated function related to the hazardous materials covered by the plan, or is responsible for implementing the plan must be trained concerning the security plan and its implementation.

notes.front: Security awareness or in-depth security training: which one does every hazmat employee receive, whether or not the employer has a security plan?
notes.back: Security awareness training. In-depth security training applies only to employees linked to a subpart I security plan.
notes.explanation: 172.704(a)(4) says “each hazmat employee”; (a)(5) is limited to employees of a person required to have a security plan.
notes.contrast: In-depth security: for employees who handle covered hazmat, perform related regulated functions or implement the security plan.
notes.source: 49 CFR 172.704(a)(4) and (a)(5) (revised as of 1 October 2025), p. 305
notes.evidence: Each hazmat employee must receive training that provides an awareness of security risks associated with hazardous materials transportation and methods designed to enhance transportation security.

notes.front: General awareness or function-specific training: which one changes when an employee moves to a different job?
notes.back: Function-specific training, because it covers requirements specifically applicable to the functions the employee performs.
notes.explanation: General awareness gives every employee the same familiarity with the HMR and hazmat recognition.
notes.contrast: General awareness/familiarization: familiarity with the HMR and recognising hazmat, for every hazmat employee.
notes.evidence: that are specifically applicable to the functions the employee performs.

notes.front: Can training given to meet Occupational Safety and Health Administration or Environmental Protection Agency hazard communication rules count towards 172.704(a)?
notes.back: Yes, to the extent it addresses the training components specified in 172.704(a).
notes.explanation: Only the parts of that training that address the 172.704(a) components count.
notes.evidence: may be used to satisfy the training requirements in paragraph (a) of this section to the extent that such training addresses the training components specified in paragraph (a) of this section.

notes.front: A plant’s workers took the hazard communication course the Occupational Safety and Health Administration requires. It covers recognising hazardous chemicals but nothing about HMR shipping duties. How far does it count?
notes.back: D: Only for the 172.704(a) components it actually addresses; the rest must still be covered.
notes.explanation: 172.704(b) lets such training satisfy 172.704(a) only to the extent it addresses the specified components.
notes.choices:
A) Fully: any federal safety course satisfies subpart H
B) Not at all: only HMR courses count
C) Fully, if the employer keeps a record of it
D) Only for the 172.704(a) components it actually addresses; the rest must still be covered
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: the credit is limited to the components the course addresses. B is wrong: 172.704(b) expressly allows such training to count. C is wrong: keeping a record does not add missing content.
notes.evidence: may be used to satisfy the training requirements in paragraph (a) of this section to the extent that such training addresses the training components specified in paragraph (a) of this section.

notes.front: Under 172.704(c)(1), how may a new or reassigned hazmat employee perform functions before training is complete?
notes.back: Only under the direct supervision of a properly trained and knowledgeable hazmat employee.
notes.explanation: This is the exception that 172.702(b) refers to; it lasts only until the training deadline.
notes.evidence: (i) The employee performs those functions under the direct supervision of a properly trained and knowledgeable hazmat employee; and

notes.front: Initial training must be completed within {{c1::90 days}} after employment or a change in job function.
notes.explanation: The same period applies to a new employee and to one who changes job functions.
notes.evidence: (ii) The training is completed within 90 days after employment or a change in job function.

notes.front: A new loader starts on Monday. Her training course is booked for five weeks later. What does 172.704(c)(1) allow meanwhile?
notes.back: B: She may load under the direct supervision of a properly trained and knowledgeable hazmat employee, if training is finished within 90 days.
notes.explanation: Both conditions in 172.704(c)(1) must be met: direct supervision, and completion within 90 days after employment.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing: she may not load at all until trained
B) She may load under the direct supervision of a properly trained and knowledgeable hazmat employee, if training is finished within 90 days
C) She may load alone for up to 90 days
D) She may load alone if she has read the HMR
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: 172.704(c)(1) lets her perform the functions before training under conditions. C is wrong: working alone breaks the direct supervision condition. D is wrong: reading is neither supervision nor training.
notes.evidence: A new hazmat employee, or a hazmat employee who changes job functions may perform those functions prior to the completion of training provided— (i) The employee performs those functions under the direct supervision of a properly trained and knowledgeable hazmat employee; and (ii) The training is completed within 90 days after employment

notes.front: A forklift driver with current training is moved to preparing shipping papers. What applies to the new function?
notes.back: D: Training for it must be completed within 90 days of the change, with direct supervision until then.
notes.explanation: 172.704(c)(1) treats an employee who changes job functions like a new employee.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing until his next three-year refresher
B) Nothing, because he is already a trained hazmat employee
C) He must stop all hazmat work until trained
D) Training for it must be completed within 90 days of the change, with direct supervision until then
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: the change of function starts its own 90-day period. B is wrong: function-specific training must match the new function. C is wrong: he may work under direct supervision until trained.
notes.evidence: (ii) The training is completed within 90 days after employment or a change in job function.

notes.front: A hazmat employee must receive the training required by subpart H at least once every {{c1::three years}}.
notes.explanation: The words are “at least once”, so three years is the longest allowed gap between trainings.
notes.evidence: (2) Recurrent training. A hazmat employee must receive the training required by this subpart at least once every three years.

notes.front: An employee last completed hazmat training in June 2023 and has had none since. By when is recurrent training due at the latest?
notes.back: A: June 2026, three years after the last training.
notes.explanation: 172.704(c)(2) requires the training at least once every three years.
notes.choices:
A) June 2026, three years after the last training
B) June 2024, one year after
C) June 2028, five years after
D) Never, if the employee stays in the same job
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: the cycle is three years, not one. C is wrong: five years exceeds the three-year maximum. D is wrong: recurrent training applies whether or not the job changes.
notes.evidence: A hazmat employee must receive the training required by this subpart at least once every three years.

notes.front: If a security plan is revised during the three-year cycle, when must in-depth security retraining happen?
notes.back: Within 90 days of implementation of the revised plan.
notes.explanation: In-depth security training otherwise follows the same three-year cycle as the other components.
notes.evidence: if the security plan for which training is required is revised during the three-year recurrent training cycle, within 90 days of implementation of the revised plan.

notes.front: A new driver’s hazmat training from her last job is relevant to her new role. Can the new employer rely on it?
notes.back: Yes, provided a current record of training is obtained from her previous employer.
notes.explanation: 172.704(c)(3) allows relevant training from a previous employer or other source, on that condition.
notes.evidence: Relevant training received from a previous employer or other source may be used to satisfy the requirements of this subpart provided a current record of training is obtained from hazmat employees’ previous employer.

notes.front: Is a hazmat employer excused from HMR requirements while an employee’s training is incomplete?
notes.back: No. Each hazmat employer is responsible for compliance regardless of whether the required training has been completed.
notes.explanation: Training does not shift responsibility for compliance away from the employer.
notes.evidence: Each hazmat employer is responsible for compliance with the requirements of this subchapter regardless of whether the

notes.front: An untrained new starter, working under supervision in his first month, mislabels a package. The employer says it cannot be blamed because his 90 days are not up. Is that right?
notes.back: C: No: the employer is responsible for compliance whether or not training has been completed.
notes.explanation: 172.704(c)(4) keeps the employer responsible for compliance regardless of whether training has been completed.
notes.choices:
A) Yes: the 90-day period excuses errors
B) Yes, if the supervisor was trained
C) No: the employer is responsible for compliance whether or not training has been completed
D) Only the employee is responsible
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: the 90 days allow supervised work before training; they do not excuse non-compliance. B is wrong: supervision is a condition of working untrained, not a defence. D is wrong: 172.704(c)(4) places responsibility on the employer.
notes.evidence: Each hazmat employer is responsible for compliance with the requirements of this subchapter regardless of whether the

notes.front: Initial training and security awareness both carry a 90-day limit. What starts the clock for each?
notes.back: Initial training: employment or a change in job function. Security awareness: employment.
notes.explanation: A job change restarts the initial-training period but is not named for security awareness training.
notes.contrast: Security awareness (172.704(a)(4)): new hazmat employees within 90 days after employment.
notes.evidence: (ii) The training is completed within 90 days after employment or a change in job function.

notes.front: How long must a hazmat employer keep an employee’s training record?
notes.back: For as long as the employee works for that employer as a hazmat employee, and for 90 days after.
notes.explanation: The record must also cover the employee’s current training for the preceding three years.
notes.evidence: Each hazmat employer must create and retain a record of current training of each hazmat employee, inclusive of the preceding three years, in accordance with this section for as long as that employee is employed by that employer as a hazmat employee and for 90 days thereafter.

notes.front: To whom must a hazmat employer make an employee’s training record available on request?
notes.back: An authorised official of the Department of Transportation, or of an entity explicitly granted authority to enforce the HMR.
notes.explanation: The record must be produced at a reasonable time and location.
notes.evidence: A hazmat employer must make a hazmat employee’s record of current training available upon request, at a reasonable time and location, to an authorized official of the Department of Transportation or of an entity explicitly granted authority to enforce the HMR.

notes.front: A hazmat employee leaves the company on 1 April. What must the employer do with his training record?
notes.back: C: Keep it for 90 days after he leaves.
notes.explanation: 172.704(d) requires the record to be retained during employment as a hazmat employee and for 90 days thereafter.
notes.choices:
A) Destroy it on his last day
B) Keep it for three years after he leaves
C) Keep it for 90 days after he leaves
D) Send it to the federal agency
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: retention continues after employment ends. B is wrong: three years is how far back the record reaches, not how long it is kept after leaving. D is wrong: the employer keeps it and shows it on request.
notes.evidence: for as long as that employee is employed by that employer as a hazmat employee and for 90 days thereafter.

notes.front: The first item a training record must include is {{c1::the hazmat employee’s name}}.
notes.explanation: 172.704(d) requires a record for each hazmat employee.
notes.evidence: The record must include: (1) The hazmat employee’s name;

notes.front: A training record must include the {{c1::most recent training completion date}} of the hazmat employee’s training.
notes.explanation: It is the latest completion date that the record must show.
notes.evidence: (2) The most recent training completion date of the hazmat employee’s training;

notes.front: A training record must include a description, copy, or {{c1::the location}} of the training materials used to meet 172.704(a).
notes.explanation: The employer may describe, copy or point to the materials; any of the three meets the item.
notes.evidence: (3) A description, copy, or the location of the training materials used to meet the requirements in paragraph (a) of this section;

notes.front: A training record must include the name and {{c1::address}} of the person providing the training.
notes.explanation: Training may come from the employer or from other public or private sources (172.702(c)), and the record names which.
notes.evidence: (4) The name and address of the person providing the training; and

notes.front: A training record must include certification that the hazmat employee has been {{c1::trained and tested}}, as subpart H requires.
notes.explanation: The certification covers testing as well as training, matching the two duties in 172.702.
notes.evidence: (5) Certification that the hazmat employee has been trained and tested, as required by this subpart.

notes.front: A training record lists the employee’s name, completion date, the materials used and the trainer’s name and address. What is missing?
notes.back: A: Certification that the employee has been trained and tested.
notes.explanation: 172.704(d) lists five contents, and the fifth is that certification.
notes.choices:
A) Certification that the employee has been trained and tested
B) The employee’s home address
C) The employee’s test score as a percentage
D) The date of the employee’s first ever training
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: the address required is the trainer’s, not the employee’s. C is wrong: no score is required. D is wrong: the record needs the most recent completion date.
notes.evidence: (5) Certification that the hazmat employee has been trained and tested, as required by this subpart.

notes.front: Three years appears twice in 172.704. What does each refer to?
notes.back: The maximum interval between trainings (recurrent), and how far back the training record must reach.
notes.explanation: 172.704(c)(2) sets the cycle; 172.704(d) requires a record inclusive of the preceding three years.
notes.contrast: Record retention after leaving is 90 days, not three years.
notes.evidence: must create and retain a record of current training of each hazmat employee, inclusive of the preceding three years

notes.front: Since 13 February 2026, which training components is a packaging-only hazmat employee not subject to?
notes.back: Safety training (172.704(a)(3)) and security awareness training (172.704(a)(4)).
notes.explanation: The amended text adds security awareness to the exception, which the 10-1-25 edition limited to safety training.
notes.source: Hazardous Materials: Eliminating Unnecessary Regulatory Burdens on Fuel Transportation, final rule, 91 FR 1433 (14 January 2026), amendment to 172.704(e)(1), p. 15
notes.evidence: qualified for use in the transportation of hazardous materials, and who does not perform any other function subject to the requirements of this subchapter, is not subject to the training requirements of paragraphs (a)(3) and (a)(4) of this section.

notes.front: Under the 2026 amendment, which employees count as “packaging-only” for the 172.704(e)(1) exception?
notes.back: Those who manufacture, repair, modify, recondition or test packagings and do not offer or transport hazmat or perform any other HMR function.
notes.explanation: The 2026 rule widened the group of excepted employees to include package manufacturers.
notes.source: Hazardous Materials: Eliminating Unnecessary Regulatory Burdens on Fuel Transportation, final rule, 91 FR 1433 (14 January 2026), section-by-section discussion of 172.704, p. 12
notes.evidence: These employees are responsible for manufacturing, repairing, modifying, reconditioning, or testing packagings and do not offer or transport hazardous materials. PHMSA is also expanding the eligibility of hazmat employees excepted from safety and security trainings to include package

notes.front: The 2026 final rule that widened the packaging-only training exception took effect on {{c1::13 February 2026}}.
notes.explanation: The govinfo edition revised as of 1 October 2025 predates it, so it still prints the older exception.
notes.source: Hazardous Materials: Eliminating Unnecessary Regulatory Burdens on Fuel Transportation, final rule, 91 FR 1433 (14 January 2026), dates, p. 1
notes.evidence: DATES: Effective Date: This rule is effective February 13, 2026.

notes.front: The 10-1-25 edition text of 172.704(e)(1) and the text in force since 13 February 2026: how do they differ?
notes.back: The old text excepted repairers, modifiers, reconditioners and testers from safety training only; the new one adds manufacturers and security awareness training.
notes.explanation: The 10-1-25 edition was printed before the 2026 amendment, so it shows only the (a)(3) exception.
notes.contrast: From 13 February 2026: manufactures, repairs, modifies, reconditions or tests; not subject to (a)(3) and (a)(4).
notes.evidence: (1) A hazmat employee who repairs, modifies, reconditions, or tests packagings, as qualified for use in the transportation of hazardous materials, and who does not perform any other function subject to the requirements of this subchapter, is not subject to the training requirement of paragraph (a)(3) of this section.

notes.front: In September 2026, a worker only manufactures drums sold as qualified for hazmat and does no other HMR function. His employer has no security plan. Which components must his training include?
notes.back: A: General awareness/familiarization and function-specific training.
notes.explanation: Since 13 February 2026 he is not subject to (a)(3) and (a)(4), and in-depth security applies only with a security plan.
notes.choices:
A) General awareness/familiarization and function-specific training
B) General awareness, function-specific and safety training, but not security awareness
C) None, because he never ships hazmat
D) All five components
notes.choicesExplained: D is wrong: the amended exception removes safety and security awareness, and in-depth security needs a security plan. B is wrong: since 13 February 2026, safety training is also excepted for packaging-only employees. C is wrong: he is still a hazmat employee, and the exception removes only two components.
notes.source: Hazardous Materials: Eliminating Unnecessary Regulatory Burdens on Fuel Transportation, final rule, 91 FR 1433 (14 January 2026), amendment to 172.704(e)(1), p. 15
notes.evidence: and who does not perform any other function subject to the requirements of this subchapter, is not subject to the training requirements of paragraphs (a)(3) and (a)(4) of this section.

notes.front: A railroad signalman performs no function subject to the HMR. Which training components is he not subject to?
notes.back: Function-specific (a)(2), security awareness (a)(4) and in-depth security (a)(5).
notes.explanation: The definition of hazmat employee names railroad signalmen and maintenance-of-way employees, and 172.704(e)(2) limits the training they need.
notes.evidence: (2) A railroad maintenance-of-way employee or railroad signalman, who does not perform any function subject to the requirements of this subchapter, is not subject to the training requirements of paragraphs (a)(2), (a)(4), or (a)(5) of this section.

notes.front: Under 177.800(c), when may a carrier transport hazmat by motor vehicle?
notes.back: Only when each of its hazmat employees involved is trained as required by part 177 and subpart H of part 172.
notes.explanation: Highway carriers must meet both the general training subpart and the highway-specific rules.
notes.evidence: A carrier may not transport a hazardous material by motor vehicle unless each of its hazmat employees involved in that transportation is trained as required by this part and subpart H of part 172 of this subchapter.

notes.front: The first subject of driver training under 177.816(a) is the {{c1::pre-trip safety inspection}}.
notes.explanation: It opens the list of six subjects, before vehicle controls and operation.
notes.evidence: (1) Pre-trip safety inspection;

notes.front: Driver training includes use of vehicle controls and equipment, including operation of {{c1::emergency equipment}}.
notes.explanation: Emergency equipment is named inside the controls subject, not left to safety training alone.
notes.evidence: (2) Use of vehicle controls and equipment, including operation of emergency equipment;

notes.front: Driver training includes procedures for maneuvering {{c1::tunnels, bridges, and railroad crossings}}.
notes.explanation: These are the fourth subject, separate from general vehicle operation.
notes.evidence: (4) Procedures for maneuvering tunnels, bridges, and railroad crossings;

notes.front: Driver training includes requirements on attendance of vehicles, parking, smoking, routing and {{c1::incident reporting}}.
notes.explanation: These are operating rules for a vehicle carrying hazmat, grouped as the fifth subject.
notes.evidence: (5) Requirements pertaining to attendance of vehicles, parking, smoking, routing, and incident reporting; and

notes.front: The third driver-training subject is vehicle operation. What are two of the manoeuvres it lists?
notes.back: Any two: turning; backing; braking; parking; handling.
notes.explanation: The subject also covers vehicle characteristics that affect stability.
notes.evidence: (3) Operation of vehicle, including turning, backing, braking, parking, handling, and vehicle characteristics including those that affect vehicle stability

notes.front: The sixth driver-training subject is loading and unloading. What are two of the three items it includes?
notes.back: Any two: compatibility and segregation of cargo in a mixed load; package handling methods; load securement.
notes.explanation: These three items appear as sub-points under loading and unloading of materials.
notes.evidence: (6) Loading and unloading of materials, including— (i) Compatibility and segregation of cargo in a mixed load; (ii) Package handling methods; and (iii) Load securement.

notes.front: Who needs specialised training under 177.816(b), on top of the general driver training?
notes.back: Each person who operates a cargo tank or a vehicle with a portable tank with a capacity of 1,000 gallons or more.
notes.explanation: They must also hold the appropriate State-issued commercial driver’s license required by part 383.
notes.evidence: each person who operates a cargo tank or a vehicle with a portable tank with a capacity of 1,000 gallons or more must receive training applicable to the requirements of this subchapter and have the appropriate State-issued commercial driver’s license required by 49 CFR part 383.

notes.front: A tanker driver meets the current Commercial Driver’s License requirements with a tank vehicle endorsement. Can that satisfy the 177.816(a) and (b) training?
notes.back: Yes. Under 177.816(c), compliance with current Commercial Driver’s License requirements with a tank vehicle or hazmat endorsement may satisfy it.
notes.explanation: The rule says “may be satisfied”, and it names either a tank vehicle or a hazardous materials endorsement.
notes.evidence: (c) The training required by paragraphs (a) and (b) of this section may be satisfied by compliance with the current requirements for a Commercial Driver’s License (CDL) with a tank vehicle or hazardous materials endorsement.

notes.front: A driver’s course covers how to cross railroad crossings and bridges safely with a hazmat load. Which 177.816(a) subject is that?
notes.back: A: Procedures for maneuvering tunnels, bridges and railroad crossings.
notes.explanation: Tunnels, bridges and railroad crossings are grouped as their own subject in 177.816(a)(4).
notes.choices:
A) Procedures for maneuvering tunnels, bridges and railroad crossings
B) Loading and unloading of materials
C) Pre-trip safety inspection
D) Use of vehicle controls and equipment
notes.choicesExplained: C is wrong: the inspection happens before the trip. B is wrong: that covers compatibility, handling and securement of the load. D is wrong: controls and equipment are a separate subject.
notes.evidence: (4) Procedures for maneuvering tunnels, bridges, and railroad crossings;

notes.front: In the 10-1-25 text of 107.329, what is the minimum civil penalty for a violation relating to training?
notes.back: $617. Other hazmat violations have no minimum civil penalty.
notes.explanation: Training is the one exception the section makes to its rule of no minimum civil penalty.
notes.evidence: There is no minimum civil penalty, except for a minimum civil penalty of $617 for violations relating to training.

notes.front: An inspector finds that a shipper never trained its packers. Under the 10-1-25 text of 107.329, what is the lowest civil penalty for that violation?
notes.explanation: Violations relating to training carry a minimum civil penalty, unlike other violations.
notes.choices:
A) $617
B) There is no minimum
C) $6,170
D) $61.70
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: training violations are the stated exception to the no-minimum rule. C and D are wrong: they are not the figure in the 10-1-25 text.
notes.evidence: There is no minimum civil penalty, except for a minimum civil penalty of $617 for violations relating to training.
